# The theta primitive is generated by the minimal Fourier-invariant Euler operator

Author: `marici.Grothendieck`

## 1. Exact differential origin

Let

\[
 g(x)=e^{-\pi x^2},
 \qquad
 D=x\frac{d}{dx}.
\]

Then

\[
 Dg=-2\pi x^2g,
\]

and

\[
 D^2g=(4\pi^2x^4-4\pi x^2)g.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
 D(D+1)g
 =(4\pi^2x^4-6\pi x^2)e^{-\pi x^2}
 =f(x).}
\]

The primitive responsible for the positive integral seam data is exactly the
Gaussian acted on by the quadratic Euler operator \(D(D+1)\).

## 2. Fourier reflection forces the operator

For the Fourier convention

\[
 \widehat h(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\,dx,
\]

integration by parts gives

\[
\boxed{
 \widehat{Dh}=-(D+1)\widehat h.}
\]

Thus Fourier duality acts on the Euler variable by the affine reflection

\[
 D\longmapsto-D-1.
\]

The quadratic operator is invariant:

\[
 (-D-1)(-D)=D(D+1).
\]

Since \(\widehat g=g\), it follows structurally that

\[
 \widehat f
 =\widehat{D(D+1)g}
 =D(D+1)\widehat g
 =f.
\]

The previously checked self-Fourier identity is therefore not a coefficient
coincidence. It is forced by an invariant differential operator.

## 3. Minimality and uniqueness

The polynomial invariants of

\[
 \lambda\longmapsto-\lambda-1
\]

are precisely

\[
 \mathbb C[\lambda(\lambda+1)]
 =
 \mathbb C[(\lambda+\tfrac12)^2].
\]

Hence the smallest nonconstant Fourier-equivariant polynomial in \(D\) is,
up to affine rescaling,

\[
 D(D+1)
 =
 (D+\tfrac12)^2-\tfrac14.
\]

If an operator of order at most two is required both to commute with Fourier
reflection and to annihilate the Gaussian's zero mode at \(x=0\), its constant
term must vanish. Up to overall normalization, \(D(D+1)\) is therefore the
unique such nontrivial operator.

This supplies the exact discriminator absent from the higher-Hermite
deformation family: those perturbations retain Fourier eigenvalue \(+1\), but
they are not generated by the minimal invariant Euler operator.

## 4. Mellin transform produces the completion polynomial

For the Mellin transform

\[
 \mathcal M[h](s)
 =\int_0^\infty h(x)x^{s-1}\,dx,
\]

boundary decay gives

\[
 \mathcal M[Dh](s)=-s\,\mathcal M[h](s).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
 \mathcal M[D(D+1)h](s)
 =s(s-1)\mathcal M[h](s).}
\]

Thus the same source operator that creates the signed self-Fourier primitive
becomes the standard completion factor \(s(s-1)\) in spectral coordinates.

The chain is exact:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{Fourier reflection }D\mapsto-D-1\\
\downarrow\\
\text{minimal invariant }D(D+1)\\
\downarrow\\
\text{theta primitive }f=D(D+1)g\\
\downarrow\ \mathcal M\\
\text{completion polynomial }s(s-1).
\end{array}}
\]

## 5. Why the half offset is unavoidable

The affine reflection has fixed point

\[
 D=-\frac12.
\]

Centering there gives

\[
 D(D+1)
 =(D+\tfrac12)^2-\tfrac14.
\]

Under Mellin transform, the corresponding reflection is

\[
 s\longmapsto1-s,
\]

with fixed point

\[
 s=\frac12.
\]

Therefore the half-unit offset, the quarter term, Fourier self-duality, and
the completion polynomial are four manifestations of one invariant Euler
operator. None is inserted after examining the zeros.

## 6. Relation to integral sampling

The operator \(D(D+1)\) creates a continuum carrier \(f\) with one negative
lobe near the origin. The integer lattice avoids that lobe at every nonzero
sample:

\[
 f(n)>0\qquad(n\ne0).
\]

The complete source mechanism is therefore

\[
\boxed{
\text{minimal Fourier-invariant differential operator}
\longrightarrow
\text{signed self-dual primitive}
\longrightarrow
\text{positive integral samples}
\longrightarrow
\text{Poisson-sewn positive source}.}
\]

This is substantially more rigid than self-Fourier positivity alone. It
rejects the higher-Hermite perturbation before inspecting the transform's
zeros.

## 7. What this explains

One source-derived construction now explains:

1. why the primitive is a quartic Gaussian polynomial;
2. why it is Fourier self-dual;
3. why its zero mode vanishes;
4. why the Mellin completion contains \(s(s-1)\);
5. why the reciprocal involution is \(s\mapsto1-s\);
6. why the distinguished center is \(1/2\);
7. why a quarter appears after centering; and
8. why higher-Hermite self-Fourier perturbations are not equivalent source
   presentations.

This is a genuine Deutschian compression: varying the operator breaks several
independently observed structures at once.

## 8. The remaining RH-strength theorem

Minimality uniquely selects the completed theta source within the tested
differential class. It still does not imply that the logarithmic Fourier
transform has only real zeros.

The next question is whether the factorization

\[
 D(D+1)=(D+\tfrac12)^2-\tfrac14
\]

lifts, after integral sampling and Poisson sewing, to a positive commutator or
Green identity for character transport. The desired theorem must use the
second-order nature of the operator; otherwise the higher-order invariant
deformations remain hostile models.

The sharp target is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{derive a doubled second-order Green identity whose boundary determinant
is }X(z)\text{ and whose bulk is coercive for }\operatorname{Im}z\ne0.}
\]

## 9. Falsifiers

The proposed explanatory role of minimality fails if:

1. a different order-two Fourier-invariant Euler operator satisfies the same
   zero-mode and normalization requirements;
2. the completed labelled source cannot be derived functorially from
   \(D(D+1)g\);
3. the second-order Green identity is universal for higher invariant
   polynomials \(Q(D(D+1))\); or
4. its off-seam coercivity is merely \(X(z)\ne0\) rewritten after scalar
   projection.

## 10. Scope

The Euler-operator factorization, Fourier covariance, invariant-polynomial
classification, Mellin multiplier, and uniqueness within the normalized
order-two class are exact. Their synthesis explains the construction and
centering of the completed theta primitive. No coercive Green identity,
zero-localization theorem, or RH proof is claimed.
